subject: Career
title: The Hybrid Dilemma
description: A fast breakdown of The Hybrid Dilemma for builders.

hook.text: Hybrid sounds like the best of both worlds. In practice, it often creates the worst of both.

buildup.text: Hybrid teams face 'proximity bias' — in-office workers get more visibility, promotions, and mentorship.

discovery.text: Research shows hybrid meetings default to in-room dynamics. Remote participants become observers.

twist.text: The fix isn't forcing everyone to an office. It's designing for remote-first, even when some are co-located.

climax.text: Remote-first means: all decisions documented, all meetings accessible, all communication async-friendly.

punchline.text: Hybrid works when remote is the default, not the exception.

quiz.question: What is 'proximity bias' in hybrid work?
options: In-office workers get more visibility, promotions, and mentorship
Everyone prefers being close to others

details.summary: The hybrid dilemma describes the structural tension when some team members are in the office and others are remote, creating two classes of participants. In-person attendees naturally dominate meetings and decisions, disadvantaging remote members.
details.whyItMatters: If hybrid creates a two-tier system, remote participants become second-class team members who miss informal conversations and relationship building, undermining the equity goals of flexible work.
takeaways: Default to video calls even when some people are co-located to equalize access
Ensure decisions and discussions are documented in shared digital spaces
Monitor promotion rates between remote and in-office workers for bias

faq.question: How do you prevent remote workers from being disadvantaged in hybrid meetings?
faq.answer: When any participant is remote, everyone joins from individual devices, even those in the office. Assign a remote-champion role to ensure virtual participants are called on equally. Share all materials digitally and document decisions where everyone can see them.

faq.question: Is proximity bias real in hybrid workplaces?
faq.answer: Yes. Studies show that in-office employees receive more promotions, better performance reviews, and more project assignments than equally qualified remote workers. Leaders must actively track and correct this bias through structured evaluation processes.
